Capabilities.description:
Body of `GET /api/v1/capabilities`.

# Why this endpoint exists

`openapi.json` is a build artefact describing every endpoint the software
has. Which of them an *instance* exposes is a runtime decision its operator
made, so a single-page app generated from the contract cannot know whether
to render a login button: the contract says login exists, and on this
deployment it may not.

So the contract describes the whole surface and this reports the subset in
force. It is unauthenticated, because a client needs the answer before it
can know whether logging in is possible at all.

access_log.description:
Whether this instance writes down who fetches a share.

`false` by default. When `true`, every retrieval records the visitor's
address and browser string, and the visitor is the person it happens to,
so a client should say so on the page where the share is collected.
Nothing else will.

account_password_breach_check.description:
Whether a new account password is checked against known breaches, so a
form can look it up while typing; see `GET /auth/pwned/{prefix}`.

account_password_min_length.description:
Shortest *account* password this instance accepts, so a client can say so
before the round trip, not after it.

Named for what it governs, because there are two minimums and they
differ. See
[`share_password_min_length`](Self::share_password_min_length).

account_password_requires_digit.description: Whether an account password needs a digit.

account_password_requires_mixed_case.description:
Whether an account password needs both an uppercase and a lowercase
letter. Character classes are defined on `PasswordPolicy`; a client that
classifies differently will accept passwords the server refuses.

account_password_requires_symbol.description: Whether an account password needs a symbol. A space is not one.

accounts.description:
Whether accounts exist at all on this instance.

`false` means no registration, no login and no session: the shape for a
personal instance behind a VPN.

admin.description:
Whether the administrative endpoints are mounted.

The administration front-end is a separate deployment, so this says only
that the API half is present.

anonymous_upload.description:
Whether a caller without a session may upload.

Independent of [`accounts`](Self::accounts): an instance can have
accounts *and* accept anonymous uploads, the default.

code_length.description:
Number of characters in a retrieval code on this instance
(`share.code_length`), so the page that collects one can draw the right
number of boxes. Codes already issued keep the length they had, so this
is what *new* shares get, not a promise about every code in existence.

default_expiry_hours.description:
How long a share lasts when the uploader does not choose, in hours.

The upload form needs this to say what "leave it alone" means. `null`
when this instance lets shares live forever by default.

encryption.description: Whether an upload may be end-to-end encrypted. See `docs/encryption.md`.

max_expiry_hours.description:
The longest lifetime an uploader may ask for, in hours.

`null` when there is no ceiling. A form that knows this can bound its own
control instead of offering a date the server will refuse.

max_upload_bytes.description:
Largest single file *this caller* may send, in bytes.

The narrowest of their own limit, their role's and
`server.max_body_bytes`. So an operator who raised the instance figure
for themselves does not have it reported to every stranger, and a client
is never shown a number bigger than what it may send.

password_reset.description:
Whether this instance can send a password reset link.

`false` when no relay is configured, the default. A client that
drew the "forgot password" link regardless would send people to an
endpoint answering 404, so this is the difference between a missing
feature and a broken one.

registration.description:
Who may create an account. Meaningless when
[`accounts`](Self::accounts) is `false`.

registration_requires_confirmation.description:
Whether registering sends a confirmation link instead of creating the
account outright.

`true` means `POST /auth/register` answers `202` and nothing exists
until the address is confirmed, so a client must show "check your inbox"
instead of treating the response as a sign-in. `false` means it answers
`201` with a session, as an instance sending no mail does.

share_password_min_length.description:
Shortest password an uploader may put on a share.

Lower than the account minimum by design. A share password is a second
factor on a link that is already unguessable, and it gets read out over
the phone. A form that validated share passwords against the account
rule would refuse the four-digit code the server would have accepted.

speed_test.description:
Whether this caller may run a speed test.

Per caller, not per instance: an instance can offer the test to accounts
but not visitors, and a visitor should see the same as on an instance
without the test.

storage_remaining_bytes.description:
How much room the caller has left, in bytes.

Whichever ceiling refuses them first: their own quota, then their
role's. Callers who may read instance statistics also see the instance
ceiling. `null` if none applies.

`storage.max_total_bytes` is not in everybody's answer because on a
public instance it is the operator's capacity planning, and telling
every anonymous uploader how close the disk is to full invites them to
finish it off. Their own quota is theirs to know, and a client holding
it can say so before they pick a file.

Version of the running server, for a client that wants to warn about a

current_password.description:
The current password. Required even though the caller is signed in: it

Omitted by an account without one (`has_password: false`), which is

# Why this exists

Three settings are retention periods, and shortening one means the next
sweep removes things that were going to be kept. Nothing warns about it and
nothing brings them back.

An empty "are you sure?" does not help, because everyone clicks it. A number
does: "this removes 23 shares, 4.2 GB" is a sentence that gives pause.

# What "delete" means here

Every link stops working the moment this returns. The bytes go later,
when the housekeeping pass reaches them, because removing hundreds of
objects inside one request times out half way through with no record of
where it got to. Nothing serves the content in the meantime; what
arrives after the answer is the disk space.

# Why only list endpoints have an envelope

A paged response carries the rows and facts about the collection. Without a
place for the latter, `total` ends up beside the rows under a per-endpoint
name, and clients read each list differently. Other endpoints return a
single object with nothing like that to carry, so wrapping them would only
add nesting.

expires_at.description: When it stops being served, RFC 3339.

files.description: Every file this share holds. Empty for text and for a locked share.

has_password.description: Whether a password must be presented before anything else is revealed.

key_salt.description: The salt a password-derived key is stretched with, for `password`.

scanning.description:
Whether it is waiting for the malware scanner and so cannot be
downloaded yet. `false` while locked, since a locked share reveals
nothing about its content.

sealed_details.description: The title and a note's language, sealed, on an encrypted share.

size_bytes.description: Size of the content in bytes.

unlocked.description: Whether the fields below are filled in.

uses_remaining.description: How many retrievals remain, or `null` for unlimited.

RecoveryCodesResponse.description: New recovery codes. Shown once: only their digests are kept.

recovery_codes.description: Each works once, in place of a code from the app.

name.description: What to call it. `Passkey` when omitted.

email.description: Address to reach the account at.

invite_code.description:
An invite code, on an instance that asks for one.

Ignored where registration is open, so a client does not have to know
which kind of instance it is talking to before filling in the form.
`/capabilities` says which it is.

username.description:
3–32 characters: letters, digits, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter or
digit. Stored lowercased.

RegistrationCredential.description: A new passkey, as `PublicKeyCredential.toJSON()` writes it.

RelyingPartyEntity.description: The site, as the creation options name it.

id.description: The host name the passkey is scoped to.

name.description: What the browser shows as the site's name.

RemovedSharesResponse.description: How many shares an operation ended.

removed.description:
How many were still live and are now finished.

The bytes go as the reaper reaches them, so this is not how much space
has come back.

ReplaceBackendRequest.description:
Body of `PUT /admin/storage/backends/{name}`: everything in
[`BackendRequest`] but the name, which the path gives.

capacity_bytes.description: How much it may hold. Omit or send `null` for no limit.

direct_access.description: Whether browsers may be redirected to it directly.

options.description:
Backend-specific options, passed to `object_store` unchanged. Omit to
keep the stored ones; `{}` clears them.

read_only.description: Whether it should stop taking new content.

url.description:
Where it is. Sealed before it is stored.

Without credentials, here or in `options`, the stored ones are kept,
as long as the backend stays on the same store: same scheme, same
server, same options. Moving to another bucket keeps them; moving to
another endpoint is refused until credentials are sent.

allowCredentials.description:
Always empty: the browser offers whichever passkeys it holds for the
site, and the answer says which account.

rpId.description: The host name the passkey must be scoped to.

max_file_bytes.description:
Largest single file accounts in this role may send.

Omit or send `null` to fall back to `server.max_body_bytes`; send `0`
for no limit of its own. `server.max_body_bytes` still applies on top,
so this can only lower it.

permissions.description:
Everything it should allow, as `resource:verb` strings.

The whole set, not a change to it, so two operators editing the same
role cannot interleave their edits into a set neither chose. The last
one to press save wins, visibly.

quota_bytes.description:
How much storage each account in this role may hold.

Omit or send `null` to fall back to the instance-wide ceiling; send `0`
for no ceiling at all. Those are different: `null` follows
`storage.max_total_bytes` as it changes, `0` ignores it.

RoleResponse.description: One role, as the API describes it.

description.description: What it is for, in the operator's own words.

is_system.description:
Whether it is one of the two the instance was seeded with.

Those cannot be deleted: an instance whose administrator role was
removed has no account left that could create one. They can be edited.

max_file_bytes.description:
Largest single file each account in it may send.

`null` means `server.max_body_bytes` applies; `0` means no limit here.

name.description: What an operator types and reads.

quota_bytes.description:
How much storage each account in it may hold.

`null` means the instance ceiling applies; `0` means no ceiling.

updated_at.description: When its permissions last changed, RFC 3339.

deferred.description:
Files and notes the scanner could not be reached for, served unscanned
and retried until it answers.

enabled.description:
Whether `scan.url` names a scanner. When `false` the rest says nothing
about one.

last_checked_at.description:
When it was last called, or `null` before it has been since start-up
or since `scan.url` changed.

last_error.description: Why the last call failed, or `null` when it answered.
last_error.example: could not talk to the scanner: Connection refused (os error 111)

pending.description: Files and notes waiting on their first verdict, held until it comes.

reachable.description:
Whether it answered the last time it was called, or `true` before it
has been.

Learned from the scans themselves; one left idle is sent an empty file
every fifteen minutes, and one that failed every five.

ServiceStatus.description:
Where the process is in its lifecycle.

Load balancers and `docker healthcheck` need to distinguish "still migrating"
from "draining" from "healthy"; a bare 200/500 cannot express that.

SessionResponse.description:
One sign-in, as the API describes it.

Covers sessions that are over as well as the ones that work. A person
reading this is usually asking whether anyone else has been in, and a
session
that was revoked last Tuesday is exactly what they need to see.

active.description:
Whether it still works.

Sent, not left to the client to derive from `expires_at`. A browser's
clock can be wrong by more than a session's remaining life, and
being told "this is still live" by a machine with a fast clock is how a
session that should have been revoked survives.

created_ip.description:
Where the sign-in came from, when there was an answer worth recording.

`null` on an instance that sits behind an undeclared proxy, and on
sessions that predate this being recorded.

created_user_agent.description:
The `User-Agent` the sign-in arrived with, exactly as it was sent.

Not parsed into "Chrome on macOS". Doing that reliably is famously hard,
and getting it wrong marks a session as yours when it is not.
created_user_agent.example: Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7) Safari/605.1.15

current.description:
Whether this is the session reading the list.

The one thing a person cannot work out for themselves, and the one they
need before ending anything.

ended_reason.description:
Why it ended early, if it was ended.

`null` means it simply ran out. The values are `signed_out`, `revoked`,
`password_changed`, `password_reset` and `account_disabled`.

expires_at.description: When it stops, or stopped, working.

last_seen_at.description: When this session was last used.

SettingResponse.description: One setting, as the panel draws it.

editable.description: Whether this endpoint will change it.

fallback.description:
What it would be without the panel's override: the environment's value,
or the default. Sending `null` for the key goes back to this. Masked like
`value`.

key.description: Dotted key, the same spelling the file and the environment use.

refusal.description:
Why it will not, when it will not.

`fixed_at_boot` for something the running process cannot pick up,
`secret` for something that holds a credential. Present so a screen can
explain instead of only greying the field out.

secret.description:
Whether this holds a credential this endpoint writes but never returns.

When true, `value` is a boolean saying whether one is set, never the
credential itself. A screen shows "configured" next to an empty field
instead of pre-filling something it cannot read back.

SettingsResponse.description: Everything this instance can be configured with.

ShareBody.description:
The request body of `POST /shares`: the content itself, as bytes.

A named type only so the contract can say `format: binary`. Declaring the
body as `Vec<u8>` makes utoipa emit an *array of integers*, which a docs UI
renders as a JSON array editor and a generated client types as `number[]`.

An empty body is refused with a `400`, and that cannot be expressed here.
`min_length` is field-level, and the `value_type` above overrides the
field's schema; drop it and the body stops being binary. So the handler
enforces it, and a generator reading this will think an empty body is
valid.

kind.description:
What happened: `view` or `copy`.

Retrieval is not one of these. See [`record_event`].

SharePage.description: A page of the caller's shares.

ShareResponse.description: A share as the API describes it. Never carries the content.

code.description: The retrieval code, as a person reads it.

copy_count.description: How many times a client reported it being copied.

disabled.description:
Whether it has been switched off, by an operator or because the scanner
found a threat. A disabled share answers `404` to everyone else.

encryption.description:
`link` or `password` for an end-to-end encrypted share, `null` for one
the server can read.

expires_at.description: When it stops being served, RFC 3339, or `null` to live until deleted.

files.description: Every file this share holds. Empty for text and for a locked share.

has_password.description: Whether a password must be presented to retrieve it.

key_salt.description: The salt a password-derived key was stretched with, for `password`.

last_accessed_at.description:
When it was last retrieved, RFC 3339.

Answers the question people ask of their own share: has it been picked
up yet?

management_token.description:
Token that lets an anonymous uploader delete this share.

**Shown once, at creation, and only for an anonymous upload.** Only its
digest is stored. Without it, a mistaken anonymous upload could never be
taken back.

path.description:
Where the share lives, relative to this instance's origin.

Relative by design. The server does not know what host it is reached
through, and guessing wrong behind a reverse proxy produces broken
links. The caller already knows the origin it called.

scan_detail.description:
The threat's name for `infected`; `encrypted` or `too_large` for
`skipped`.

scan_state.description:
The malware scanner's verdict, the most significant across its files:
`pending`, `clean`, `infected`, `skipped` or `deferred`. `null` when it
was never sent to a scanner. See `docs/scanning.md`.

scanning.description:
Whether it is waiting for the malware scanner. Until it is done,
downloads answer `423` with `Retry-After`.

sealed_details.description: The title and a note's language, sealed, on an encrypted share.

size_bytes.description: Size of the content in bytes.

use_count.description:
How many times it has been retrieved.

Counted by the server on the transfer path, so this is the number to
trust. The two below are what a client reported.

uses_remaining.description: How many retrievals remain, or `null` for unlimited.

view_count.description: How many times a client reported showing it.

SharedFile.description: One file in a share, as the API describes it.

position.description:
Its position in the share, from zero.

Sent explicitly, so a client that sorts or filters the list can still
restore the uploader's order.

sealed_name.description: Its name and media type, sealed, in an encrypted share.

size_bytes.description:
Its size in bytes.

For an encrypted share, the sealed size, which is what a download sends.

Source.description: Which layer a setting's value came from.

received_bytes.description: How many bytes arrived. The client times its own request and divides.

StatsDay.description: One day of what the instance held.

bytes_served.description: As `StatsResponse::bytes_served`, so it falls when a share is swept.

stored_bytes.description: As `StatsResponse::stored_bytes`, at the day's last sweep.

data.description:
One per recorded day in the range. Days the server was not running have
no entry, and history starts the day this version was first deployed.

StatsResponse.description:
What one instance is holding, at a glance.

# Why this is not a metrics endpoint

These are numbers an operator acts on: "am I near the quota", "how many
accounts are there", "is the sweep keeping up". The dashboard's one trend,
per day, is `/admin/stats/history`; anything finer belongs in Prometheus.

administrators.description: How many of those administer the instance.

bytes_redirected.description:
Bytes requested by downloads redirected straight to a store.

Requested, not delivered: the store does not report what it sent, so an
abandoned download counts in full. Kept separate so `bytes_served` still
means what left this machine.

bytes_served.description:
How many bytes this instance has sent out.

Bytes that left the process, not bytes that reached anybody: a proxy in
front holds some, and a caching CDN answers requests this never sees.
For what crossed the network, a reverse proxy's log is the authority.

Counted over the shares still here, so a swept share takes its tally
with it and this falls when one goes.

live_invites.description: How many invites could still admit an account.

live_shares.description:
How many a visitor could still open.

The gap between this and `shares` is what the sweep has not reached. A
large one means retention is longer than expected, or the sweep is not
running.

quota_bytes.description:
The ceiling from `storage.max_total_bytes`, or `null` when unset.

`null` means unset, not unlimited. On an instance taking anonymous
uploads, that combination is what the start-up warning is about.

shares.description: How many shares exist, including ones that can no longer be opened.

stored_bytes.description: Bytes of uploaded content still on the store.

StoreConfig.description:
The options that place a store, as opposed to the ones that unlock it.

An allowlist, not every option but the credentials: a key this does not
know is not sent, so a secret under a name nobody thought of stays sealed.

allow_http.description: Whether plain HTTP to the endpoint is allowed.

endpoint.description:
The server an S3-compatible store talks to (Garage, R2, `SeaweedFS`...), without
credentials, or `null` for the provider's own.

region.description: The region, when one is set.

expires_at.description: When the authorisation stops being honoured, RFC 3339.

ticket.description: Present it as `X-Share-Ticket`, or as `?t=` on a download link.

uses_remaining.description: How many retrievals remain after this one.

TokenResponse.description: An issued token, as a listing describes it. Never carries the secret.

display_prefix.description:
Leading characters of the secret, so a person can tell two tokens apart
without the service having to store either of them.

expires_at.description: When it stops being accepted, or `null` to live until revoked.

last_used_at.description: When it was last accepted, if ever.

permissions.description:
What it may do, as `resource:verb` strings.

What it was minted with, not what it can do right now. Those differ
when the owner has since been demoted, and the owner is who this list is
for. Sending the narrowed set instead would make a token look as though
it had been quietly edited.

revoked_at.description: When it was revoked, if it was.

TotpSetupResponse.description: What `POST /account/mfa/totp` answers: the secret to put in the app.

secret.description: The secret, for typing into an app that cannot scan.

uri.description: The `otpauth://` link, for a client to draw as a QR code.

current_password.description:
The current password.

Required even though the caller is signed in. Otherwise an unlocked
browser left on a desk is enough to move the account's address to one
the finder controls, after which the reset flow hands them the account.

Omitted by an account without one (`has_password: false`); see
`reauthentication_required`.

email.description:
A new address, or omitted to keep the current one.

Changing it clears the verification: the new address has not been proven
reachable, and carrying the old flag over would mean an unverified
address wearing a verified one's badge.

username.description: A new name, or omitted to keep the current one.

direct_access.description: Whether browsers may be redirected to it directly.

appearance.description:
The appearance choices, replacing whatever was stored.

Omit a field, or send `{}`, to have no opinion and follow the
instance's default. The accepted names are the ones
[`PreferencesResponse`] lists; anything else is a `400`.

changes.description:
The changes to apply, by dotted key.

`null` clears a setting, so it falls back to whichever layer comes next:
the environment, or the default. That is the only way back to a value
the panel did not choose, and why clearing is a value and not a second
endpoint.

confirm.description:
Go ahead even though the change destroys something.

Without it, a change that would remove things is refused and the answer
says what and how many. Two round trips by design: an empty "are you
sure?" is a button everyone clicks, and a number gives pause.

is_admin.description:
Whether this account administers the instance.

Omit to leave the role unchanged. Sending it always rewrites the role
(`true` to `owner`, `false` to none), so a client changing only `state`
or a quota must omit it, or it demotes the account as a side effect.

max_file_bytes.description:
Largest single file this one account may send, overriding its role's.

Absent leaves it alone, `null` clears it so the role's applies again,
and `0` gives this account no limit of its own.

`server.max_body_bytes` still applies on top; this cannot raise it.

quota_bytes.description:
A storage quota for this one account, overriding its role's.

Absent leaves it alone, `null` clears it so the role's applies again,
and `0` gives this account no ceiling of its own. Three instructions,
so absent and `null` are not the same here.

For raising or lowering one account without inventing a role for it.
`storage.max_total_bytes` still applies on top, so this cannot grant an
account more room than the instance has.

state.description:
`active` to let it in, `disabled` to suspend it.

Omitted leaves it as it is. `deleted` is refused here: removing an
account scrubs it: `DELETE`, not a field on a patch.

UploadResponse.description: A session that has just been opened.

direct.description:
Whether parts may go straight to the store instead of through here.

When `true`, `GET /uploads/{id}/parts/{number}` hands out a URL to `PUT`
each part to, and `POST /uploads/{id}/complete` finishes with the `ETag`
each `PUT` returned. `PATCH` works either way.

Depends on where this upload was placed and whether the operator has
marked that store browser-reachable, which is why it is here and not in
the capabilities: an instance with an S3 bucket and a local directory
answers differently per upload.

id.description: Identifier, and the last segment of the URL to continue at.

offset.description: How much has arrived. Zero, here.

part_size.description:
How much to send per chunk, in bytes.

A chunk that is not the last is accepted only up to a multiple of this;
the rest comes back as a lower offset and has to be re-sent. Sending
exact multiples avoids that entirely.

token.description:
Proof that a later request is the same uploader, for an anonymous one.

**Store this.** It is shown once, and without it the upload cannot be
resumed after the page is closed, the situation resuming exists for.
`null`
when the uploader is signed in, since their credential already answers.

UserEntity.description: The account, as the creation options name it.

displayName.description: Shown by the browser beside it.

id.description: An opaque handle for the account, base64url. Echoed back at sign-in.

role.description:
The role this account should be in, or `null` for none.

`null` is signed in and allowed nothing: a real state, and what an empty
list used to mean.

bearer.description: An API token from `POST /api/v1/tokens`, sent as `Authorization: Bearer tsk_…`. Shown once at creation.

session.description: Set by `POST /auth/login`. A browser sends it automatically; it is `HttpOnly`, so page scripts cannot read or set it.

They are the account's own uploads. An administrator removing another
account does not touch its content, a separate and explicit act,
but an account removing itself may say what happens to what it sent.

section 2.8 defines the refusal format. A provider that cannot parse the

against keys from the configured issuer, stands in for a credential. See

# Why this exists

Fixing everything at creation does not match how files get shared. The
link goes out, then the meeting moves, the recipient asks for another day,
or the wrong person was on the thread and the password must change now.

# Who may

The same two as `DELETE`: the owning account, or the holder of the
management token an anonymous upload was given. The permission checked is
`shares:delete`: there is no `shares:update`, and requiring the right to
delete outright is the conservative choice.

# Errors

`400` for a value the instance will not accept, `404` when the caller has no
share with that code, which is also the answer for another account's share,
since telling them apart would confirm which codes exist. `410` when the
change would revive a share whose content the sweep already removed.

# Why retrieval is not accepted here

`use_count` is a limit. A client that could report its own retrievals would
be a client deciding whether the limit applied, and one `curl` at
`/s/{code}/raw` would walk past it. The server counts that itself, on the
transfer path, where it cannot be skipped.

These two are the opposite case. Nothing reaches the server when a note is
read on screen or a copy button is pressed, so only a client can see
them. Anybody who can call this can inflate them, and that is tolerable
because nothing depends on them.

# Why it does not say whether the share exists

`204` whatever happens, including for a code that names nothing. Answering
`404` would turn an unauthenticated endpoint into a way to ask which codes
are real, the same oracle the retrieval throttle exists to close.

# Errors

`400` when `kind` is not one of the two, `429` when the source is asking too
often.

# Why files arrive one at a time

A request carrying five files loses all five when it drops at the fourth,
which is what uploading a folder of photos over a home connection runs
into. A file that fails here is retried alone.

# Why the share exists before its second file

There is no draft state. A share is created by its first file and grown by
the rest, so nothing has to be finalised, and an interrupted upload leaves a
share with what did arrive instead of nothing.

The cost is that a link opened mid-upload shows a partial share. The
uploader hands out the link afterwards.

# Errors

`400` for a name that is unusable or described the wrong way for the share,
`403` when the caller cannot show it is theirs, `404` when no share has that
code, `409` when the share holds text, `413` when the body is too large,
`507` when something is out of room. The body says whose limit it was.

# The answer must not be cached

It carries `Cache-Control: no-store`. A client that caches it anyway will
corrupt the upload: a stale offset sends the next chunk to the wrong place.
This is the one header on this endpoint that is not politeness.

# Errors

`404` when there is no such session, or the caller may not continue it. The
same answer, so a stranger cannot tell one from the other.

patch.description:
# Every chunk but the last must be a whole part

`part_size` from the `POST` is a floor, not a suggestion: a chunk that is
not the last and carries fewer bytes is refused with `400`. The object
stores this streams to will not take a part below their own minimum, five
mebibytes on S3, so a short chunk cannot be written anywhere and the offset
does not move. A client that kept sending one would loop for ever.

The last chunk is exempt, because there is nothing after it to make it whole.

A client that sends `declared_bytes` in one request never meets this at all.

# Errors

`400` when a chunk that is not the last is shorter than `part_size`, `409`
when the offset does not match, `404` when there is no such session, `415`
when the content type is not the one the specification names.

post.description:
# Where the size is checked

Here, and only here. A part URL cannot be limited to a length, so this
completes the object and then asks the store for its size. An object that
does not match the size the session declared, and was charged against the
uploader's quota, is deleted and refused.

Until then the extra bytes sit in the bucket. That is the price of not
proxying the bytes, bounded by what a session that already passed the size
and quota checks can write before this runs.

# Errors

`400` when the number of `ETag`s does not match the number of parts, or the
object did not come out the declared size. `404` when there is no such
session, `409` when this upload cannot take parts directly or already had
parts sent through this server, `410` when the session was abandoned.

get.description:
# Why

Every byte of a `PATCH` crosses this server twice, in from the uploader and
out to the bucket, and on a self-hosted instance both often share one
uplink. A part written directly to the store crosses it zero times.

# What it does not check

The part's size. The URL signs the part number and upload id, but not a
length: `object_store` refuses to sign `content-length`. So a client can
write a part of any size, which is only caught when `complete` asks the
store how large the object came out. See [`complete`].

# Errors

`404` when there is no such session or no such part, `409` when this upload
cannot take parts directly, `410` when the session was abandoned.
